profile.name: Bukcheong sajanoreum
profile.tagline: A traditional Korean lion mask dance performed to ward off evil spirits.
profile.insight: On the 15th day of the lunar New Year, dancers in Bukcheong lion masks visit wealthy homes, moving from gardens to kitchens, while children reach out to touch the lion, believing it grants them a longer life.
profile.profile: Bukcheong sajanoreum is a traditional Korean mask dance originating from the Bukcheong region of South Hamgyong Province. Designated as the 15th Important Intangible Cultural Property of Korea, the performance centers on a lion mask believed to possess the power to repel evil ghosts and secure peace for the community. The dance is deeply rooted in folk belief and historically involved competitive performances between local towns. Today, the tradition is maintained by a transmission committee formed by individuals who defected from the Bukcheong region to South Korea.
profile.profile_long: Bukcheong sajanoreum, or the Bukcheong lion play, is a significant cultural tradition originating from the Bukcheong region of South Hamgyong Province. Historically, this performance was a staple of the local community, with every region in the province participating in the practice. The dance is intrinsically linked to a folk belief system that attributes the lion with the supernatural power to turn away evil ghosts and bring peace to the household and the broader community. This cultural significance led to its formal recognition as the 15th Important Intangible Cultural Property of Korea. The performance is tied to the lunar calendar, specifically occurring on the 15th day of the New Year. The event cycle begins on the 14th night of the lunar calendar and continues until the following dawn. Before the main lion dance commences, young men from small towns engage in a preliminary activity known as torch fighting. Following this, the lion mask team visits the homes of local wealthy families. The movement through these homes is highly structured: the dancers enter the garden, proceed into the main room for dancing and eating, move into the kitchen, and finally return to the inner garden. This route is repeated throughout the visit. A notable aspect of the performance is the interaction with children; it is a common belief that children will live longer lives if they are able to touch the lion mask or pull on its hair. The competitive nature of the dance was formalized in 1930, when towns began to decorate their own unique lion masks and compete against one another. The winning team was historically awarded crops, which were then utilized for community-focused initiatives such as scholarships, relief for the poor, and support for the elderly. While some smaller or less-resourced teams have disappeared over time, the tradition remains preserved through the efforts of a transmission committee. This committee was organized in August 1960 by people who had defected to South Korea from the Bukcheong province. The designated holders of this tradition include Yun Youn-chun, Kim Su-seok, Byun Young-ho, Dong Young-suk, Yeo Je-sung, and Jeon Jung-sik. The dance continues to serve as a vital link to the heritage of the Bukcheong region, maintaining its status as a protected cultural property.

sections.origins_and_history: The dance originated in the Bukcheong region of South Hamgyong Province, rooted in folk beliefs regarding the protective power of lions. Competitive performances between local towns began in 1930, with prizes of crops used for community welfare. A transmission committee was formed in 1960 by defectors to South Korea to ensure the survival of the tradition.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance involves performers wearing a lion mask. The performance includes a route through a house, moving from the garden to the main room, then to the kitchen, and back to the inner garden. Technique not described in sources.
sections.costume_and_setting: The central costume is a lion mask. The setting includes local wealthy family homes, specifically gardens, main rooms, and kitchens.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Performed on the 15th day of the lunar New Year, starting on the 14th night. It is intended to ward off evil spirits and bring peace. Children participate by touching the lion to ensure a longer life.
sections.notable_figures: Yun Youn-chun, Kim Su-seok, Byun Young-ho, Dong Young-suk, Yeo Je-sung, and Jeon Jung-sik.
sections.regional_variants: Historically performed in every region of Bukcheong province, with particular fame in Bukcheong-eup, Gaheomyun, and Gutangcheon.
sections.lineage: Designated as the 15th Important Intangible Cultural Property of Korea.
